blocks: ## Why this matters لِمَاذَا نُحَوِّلُ الْفِعْلَ إِلَى اسْمٍ؟
Nominal derivatives let learners discuss activities, people, roles, results and states with greater range and precision.
### Core
Recognise common verbal nouns and Form I participles.
### Develop
Form and agree active/passive participles and use maṣdars in phrases.
### Stretch
Recognise derived-form patterns and weak/hamzated spelling changes.
[callout] Communication target: Use action nouns and participles naturally in sustained description and explanation.
## Diagnostic start
Identify action, doer and affected forms.
## Verbal nouns: naming the action
The maṣdar turns an action into a noun that can be a subject, object or part of a prepositional/iḍāfa phrase.

TABLE: Verb | Verbal noun | Useful phrase // كَتَبَ / يَكْتُبُ | كِتَابَةٌ | أُحِبُّ الْكِتَابَةَ. // قَرَأَ / يَقْرَأُ | قِرَاءَةٌ | الْقِرَاءَةُ مُفِيدَةٌ. // دَرَسَ / يَدْرُسُ | دِرَاسَةٌ | بَعْدَ دِرَاسَةِ النَّصِّ... // سَافَرَ / يُسَافِرُ | سَفَرٌ | أَسْتَمْتِعُ بِالسَّفَرِ. // زَارَ / يَزُورُ | زِيَارَةٌ | قُمْنَا بِزِيَارَةٍ. // تَعَلَّمَ / يَتَعَلَّمُ | تَعَلُّمٌ | تَعَلُّمُ اللُّغَاتِ مُهِمٌّ. // اِسْتَعْمَلَ / يَسْتَعْمِلُ | اِسْتِعْمَالٌ | اِسْتِعْمَالُ التِّقْنِيَّةِ.
[callout] Form I caution: The verbal noun is often not fully predictable. Store قَرَأَ / قِرَاءَةٌ، كَتَبَ / كِتَابَةٌ، زَارَ / زِيَارَةٌ as lexical pairs.
## Active participles: naming or describing the doer
Active participles can function as nouns, professions, temporary states or adjective-like descriptions.

TABLE: Verb | Active participle | Meaning/use // كَتَبَ | كَاتِبٌ / كَاتِبَةٌ | writer / writing person // لَعِبَ | لَاعِبٌ / لَاعِبَةٌ | player // قَرَأَ | قَارِئٌ / قَارِئَةٌ | reader // ذَهَبَ | ذَاهِبٌ / ذَاهِبَةٌ | going / one who is going // قَالَ | قَائِلٌ / قَائِلَةٌ | speaker / one who says // قَامَ | قَائِمٌ / قَائِمَةٌ | standing / existing depending on context
[callout] Form I pattern: Active participles commonly follow فَاعِلٌ . Hollow and hamzated verbs show spelling adjustments: قَالَ ← قَائِلٌ، قَرَأَ ← قَارِئٌ .
## Passive participles: describing the affected thing
Passive participles connect verb meaning to noun description and state.

TABLE: Verb | Passive participle | Model // كَتَبَ | مَكْتُوبٌ | رِسَالَةٌ مَكْتُوبَةٌ بِوُضُوحٍ // كَسَرَ | مَكْسُورٌ | هَاتِفٌ مَكْسُورٌ // فَتَحَ | مَفْتُوحٌ | الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ // أَغْلَقَ | مُغْلَقٌ | الْمَتْجَرُ مُغْلَقٌ // عَرَفَ | مَعْرُوفٌ | شَخْصٌ مَعْرُوفٌ // وَجَدَ | مَوْجُودٌ | الْكِتَابُ مَوْجُودٌ هُنَا // قَرَأَ | مَقْرُوءٌ | نَصٌّ مَقْرُوءٌ
[callout] Form I pattern: Passive participles commonly follow مَفْعُولٌ . Agreement works like adjectives: كِتَابٌ مَكْتُوبٌ، رِسَالَةٌ مَكْتُوبَةٌ .
## Derived forms: predictable families as Stretch
Recognise reusable nominal patterns without losing the communicative vocabulary focus.

TABLE: Form family | Verbal noun | Active participle | Passive participle // II فَعَّلَ | تَفْعِيلٌ | مُفَعِّلٌ | مُفَعَّلٌ // III فَاعَلَ | مُفَاعَلَةٌ | مُفَاعِلٌ | مُفَاعَلٌ // V تَفَعَّلَ | تَفَعُّلٌ | مُتَفَعِّلٌ | مُتَفَعَّلٌ // VIII اِفْتَعَلَ | اِفْتِعَالٌ | مُفْتَعِلٌ | مُفْتَعَلٌ // X اِسْتَفْعَلَ | اِسْتِفْعَالٌ | مُسْتَفْعِلٌ | مُسْتَفْعَلٌ

[callout/warning] Stretch, not a memorisation wall: Derived forms are more predictable than Form I, but learners should meet them through useful vocabulary: تَعَلُّمٌ، مُتَعَلِّمٌ، اِسْتِعْمَالٌ، مُسْتَعْمِلٌ، مُسْتَعْمَلٌ .
[example] يَسْتَعْمِلُ الطَّالِبُ الْحَاسُوبَ. → الطَّالِبُ مُسْتَعْمِلٌ، وَالْحَاسُوبُ مُسْتَعْمَلٌ.
[ar] يَسْتَعْمِلُ الطَّالِبُ الْحَاسُوبَ.
[ar] الطَّالِبُ مُسْتَعْمِلٌ، وَالْحَاسُوبُ مُسْتَعْمَلٌ.
## Nominal-form misconception clinic
A useful correction explains the form, not only the answer.
### Action versus doer
✗ أُحِبُّ الْكَاتِبَ بمعنى I love writing
✓ أُحِبُّ الْكِتَابَةَ
The maṣdar names the activity; الكاتب names a writer.
### Doer versus affected
✗ هَذَا رِسَالَةٌ كَاتِبَةٌ
✓ هَذِهِ رِسَالَةٌ مَكْتُوبَةٌ
The letter is affected by writing and requires feminine agreement.
### Form I prediction
✗ كُلُّ مَصْدَرٍ عَلَى وَزْنٍ وَاحِدٍ
✓ مَصَادِرُ الْبَابِ الْأَوَّلِ تُتَعَلَّمُ مَعَ الْفِعْلِ
Form I maṣdars are lexically varied.
### Non-human agreement
✗ الْكُتُبُ مَكْتُوبُونَ
✓ الْكُتُبُ مَكْتُوبَةٌ
Non-human plural takes feminine singular agreement.
## Replayable classification game
Sort each form by its grammatical meaning.
## Apply the grammar across skills
Grammar becomes useful when it helps you understand and communicate.
### 📖 Reading workshop
Read a profile and classify every nominal derivative as action, doer or affected state.
### 🎧 Listening workshop
Listen to pairs such as كتابة/كاتب/مكتوب and identify which meaning the speaker intends.
### 🗣️ Speaking workshop
Describe yourself as a learner and discuss activities you enjoy using verbal nouns and participles.
### 🛠️ Editing workshop
Repair confusion between maṣdar and participle, wrong feminine agreement and non-human plural agreement.
### ✍️ Integrated production task
Write 130–140 words about learning, reading, sport or technology. Use at least four verbal nouns, four active participles and four passive participles.
[callout] Model: تَعَلُّمُ اللُّغَاتِ نَشَاطٌ مُفِيدٌ. أَنَا مُتَعَلِّمَةٌ مُجْتَهِدَةٌ، وَأُحِبُّ الْقِرَاءَةَ وَالْكِتَابَةَ. فِي مَكْتَبَتِنَا كُتُبٌ مَعْرُوفَةٌ وَنُصُوصٌ مَقْرُوءَةٌ بِعِنَايَةٍ.
[callout] Success checklist: Distinguish action, doer and affected meaning; apply gender and non-human plural agreement; include one Form I and one derived-form family.
Save and mark complete Clear
Plan the verb changes as a timeline, root map or sentence flowchart. Label each form in Arabic.
Use three colours or symbols: circle verbal nouns, underline active participles, box passive participles. Add arrows to the nouns they describe.
## Final mastery check
Distinguish and form the three main nominal derivatives.
### Lesson mastery summary
- recognise and use common verbal nouns;
- form high-frequency Form I active participles;
- form and agree high-frequency passive participles;
- recognise useful derived-form nominal patterns.
Return in 3–7 days and repeat the final check without reviewing first. Retrieval, not recognition alone, builds secure verb control.
